newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey may import wheat after Argentine crop out.
newsitem.headline: Turkey may import wheat after Argentine crop out.

text.p: Turkey may import an unspecified amount of wheat to control bread prices after the Argentine grain crop comes on to the market next month, Agriculture Minister Musa Demirci said on Tuesday.
Bread prices have risen 30 percent in the past three weeks.
"(The) grain harvest in Argentine ... will begin next month and, if need be, wheat will then be imported and bread prices will be adjusted," he told parliament.
He said the Turkish Grain Board (TMO) had enough wheat in its stocks, but imports would be necessary to control wheat prices.

"Turkey produced 18.5 million tonnes this season. The TMO has 1.3 million tonnes of this and the remainder is held by either farmers or traders," he said, after being asked by an MP for a briefing on the status of bread and wheat prices.
"We will not have a wheat shortage," he said.
The TMO's stocks include 500,000 tonnes of durum wheat it has purchased from farmers so far, according to officials.
Western traders and local analysts say Turkey's 1996/97 wheat crop can not exceed 16.5 million tonnes, despite the official estimate of 18.5 million tonnes.
Officials and traders said earlier Turkey's import plans, which it declared two weeks ago, might be put on hold for sometime because of a recent decline in wheat prices.

Turkey has been considering wheat imports after bread and wheat prices rose by about 30 percent locally following clampdown due to a zero-tolerance requirement on wheat imports from the United States on grounds they might contain ergot fungus.
Local wheat prices surged to 27,000 lira per kg from 20,000 lira after the restriction on the imported U.S. wheat.
The United States then suspended issuing health certificates for exports to Turkey, virtually banning sales of wheat and several other grains to Turkey.
Turkey later eased the zero-tolerance requirement to 0.05 percent for ergot fungus -- a level seen as the world standard for the fungus.
But this was not found satisfactory by the United States, which last week said Turkey was now applying the zero-tolerance policy for other disease types.
Another government attempt last week to let the TMO sell from its stocks without profits eased the wheat prices to levels of 23,000 lira.
Turkey's import intention caused wheat prices to surge in international commodity markets.
But Turkish officials have failed to announce a firm date to tender for the required wheat.

A further statement by agriculture officials last week that the government was planning a decree to cut a 15-percent wheat import tax, imposed in September to limit imports after a bigger harvest this year, has also contributed to speculation that Turkey will import fairly soon.
The agricultural official abstained to comment on the status of the decree, which would enable the TMO, private traders and millers to import at cheaper prices.
Traders earlier said November was unfavourable for Turkey for importing wheat and a possible decrease in international prices next month would be more viable for Turkey.
-- Ercan Ersoy, Ankara Newsroom, 90-312-4462940
